title: Calamari Fritti
subtitle: Crispy fried squid rings with lemon
excerpt: Calamari fritti is the Italian way of frying squid -- a light coating of seasoned flour and a quick dip in hot oil. The result is golden, crisp, and completely unlike the rubbery version served in most restaurants. Serve immediately with plenty of lemon.
sourceNotes: Fried squid is eaten all along the Italian coastline from Venice to Sicily. The flour-only coating is the Roman and southern Italian method -- no egg, no breadcrumbs.

content.text: The oil must be at 180C before the squid goes in. Too cool and the coating soaks up oil and turns greasy.

items.prepNote: use 500g cleaned squid, cut into rings
seasoned with salt and black pepper

content.text: Pat the squid rings very dry with kitchen paper. Any moisture will make the oil spit.
Pour the oil into a large saucepan to a depth of about 8cm. Heat to 180C over a medium-high flame.
Put the seasoned flour in a bowl. Toss the squid in the flour a handful at a time. Shake off any excess.
Fry in small batches for 2 minutes each, turning once, until golden and crisp. Do not crowd the pan.
Lift out with a slotted spoon onto kitchen paper. Season immediately with salt flakes.
Scatter over the chopped parsley and serve at once with lemon wedges.

items.symptom: The squid is chewy and tough
items.cause: It cooked for too long. Squid turns rubbery past the 2-3 minute mark.
items.fix: Keep batches small and the time short. Very large rings can be scored to help them cook evenly.

items.symptom: The coating falls off in the oil
items.cause: The squid was too wet when it went into the flour.
items.fix: Dry the squid thoroughly before flouring. Do not let it sit after coating -- fry immediately.

items.symptom: The oil is smoking and splashing
items.cause: The temperature is too high, or the squid carried in water.
items.fix: Reduce the heat slightly and always pat squid dry. Use a deep pan with high sides for safety.

content.text: Calamari fritti appears on every coastal trattoria menu in Italy. Romans eat it on Fridays as part of the fritto misto tradition. Street stalls in Naples and Palermo serve it in paper cones. The dish is best eaten standing up, hot from the pan.
